newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh pension law threatens air traffic safety. [corrected 09:10 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Kazakh pension law threatens air traffic safety. [corrected 09:10 gmt]

text.p: Kazakhstan's new pension law, raising the retirement age for air traffic controllers by 13 years to 63, could threaten the safety of air traffic over the former Soviet state, Kazakh and foreign controllers said on Friday.

"This new law is a very big concern for our federation, because the retirement age for controllers shouldn't be beyond 55," Gunter Melchert, Executive Vice-President in Europe for the International Federation of Air Traffic Controllers Associations (IFATCA), told Reuters.
"This is a very severe problem, because it could be detrimental to safety," he added.

Melchert's visit to the Kazakh capital Almaty was prompted by a recently-adopted new pension law which increases the legal retirement age in Kazakhstan by three (corrects from five) years to 58 years for women and by 3 (corrects from 13) years to 63 years for men.

The government of the improverished Central Asian state, which views reforming the national pension system as a major economic boon with a quickly ageing population, has excluded air traffic controllers from a group of privileged professions with lower retirement ages.
IFATCA says 50-55 years should be the retirement age limit for controllers, who are exposed to constant stress and whose health and reaction speed deteriorate with time.
Kazaeronavigatsia, the state company in charge of air traffic control which employs around 800 controllers nationwide, is among the strongest critics of the new law.

"According to international statistics, blunders of air traffic controllers and pilots account for 63 percent of all accidents in the air...But the government explains the adoption of this law by the difficult economic situation," said Vitaly Medvedev, chairman of Kazaeronavigatsia's trade union.

Kazakhstan has witnessed five major air accidents in the last 15 years. One of them, claiming about 80 victims when a Tupolev-134 plane hit a mountain near Almaty in 1983, was blamed on a controller, who was later sentenced to 12 years in prison.
Controllers, who in Soviet times were treated as privileged workers able to retire at 50, are afraid it would take a new disaster to reestablish the original retirement age.
Russia and other countries of the former Soviet Union have left the retirement age of 50 years for their air traffic controllers unchanged.
Controllers held talks with the government on Thursday.
